title: Pink Noise Brings Better Brain-Protecting Sleep
paragraphs: When you sleep, your brain clears out waste products such as old proteins that build up during the day.

This happens because those waste products are washed away by waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) — a clear liquid that also cushions the brain and spinal cord. This helps keep the brain healthy and protects it against dementia.
CSF waves are at their strongest during deep sleep. They are closely linked to a type of brain activity called slow waves, which are also strongest during this phase of sleep.
Now a new study published in Science Translational Medicine has found that pink noise may strengthen those CSF waves, leading to more restorative sleep.

Pink noise is sometimes called ambient noise, and it can be used to filter out other distractions. It uses a consistent frequency to create a flat, even sound that can be very relaxing, and often sounds a bit like steady rain or a distant waterfall.
The study monitored the brains of 14 people while they slept. When the participants reached deep sleep, the researchers played short, 50-millisecond bursts of pink noise.
This was played quietly enough that, even though the brain registered the sound, the pink noise didn't wake anyone up.
The researchers found that pink noise seemed to increase both the strength of the brain-cleaning CSF waves during deep sleep and the associated slow wave brain activity.
The brain scans also showed how slow waves stimulated blood vessels in the brain, causing them to constrict and dilate and act like a pump driving CSF out of the brain along with waste.
The researchers now want to find out if improving CSF flow like this could help people get more restorative sleep outside of a lab setting. This could be especially helpful for people with insomnia.
They also want to look at whether improving this waste-removal process could help people already experiencing dementia by reducing the buildup of harmful proteins in their brains.
